extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners working on patent analysis and NLP (including patent examiners, patent attorneys, and AI researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Survey of NLP/ML tasks and methodological criteria for assessing patent-related properties (novelty, patentability, granting, litigation, valuation, forecasting, recommendation, and text generation). Guides what signals, data, and modelling choices matter for automated patent assessment and generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (legal definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent novelty: the invention has not been known or used in the prior art; novelty focuses on the invention’s features compared to the prior art in a legal context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate this legal concept from technological novelty/originality; assessment should compare specific features (claims) against prior art disclosures rather than relying on generic texts like titles/abstracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological novelty / originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Technological novelty/originality refers to the advancement and uniqueness of the technological contribution in a technical context (distinct from legal novelty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be operationalized via dimensions such as novelty in recombination, novelty in technological origins, and novelty in scientific origins (Verhoeven et al. 2016). Measures used include citation-based proximity indicators, co-citation, cosine similarity, co-occurrence, and co-classification; note that technological novelty may convey different information than legal novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicator-based novelty scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pre-defined indicators (e.g., citations, classification codes, proximity measures) with scores/weights to compute a novelty score relative to prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers must select and weight indicators carefully; selection/weighting can be subjective and indicators may not capture nuanced aspects of inventions. Normalization methods are often used to balance different indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outlier detection for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat potentially novel inventions as outliers in a patent landscape by representing patents via text embeddings and applying outlier-detection algorithms (e.g., Local Outlier Factor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May not align with legal novelty because embeddings/distance may not represent feature differences; can flag unusual but non-novel patents (statistical outliers without meaningful technical novelty). Using claims as input (rather than titles/abstracts) and explicit feature extraction (e.g., via LLMs) is recommended to better align with legal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity-based novelty measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute similarity between the target patent and existing patents (using embeddings, high-dimensional keyword frequency vectors, cosine similarity, Euclidean distance); patents with low similarity scores are considered more novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent titles and abstracts are often generic and may fail to disclose features needed for legal novelty assessment. Similarity can reflect technological impact rather than legal novelty; high-dimensional keyword representations can capture different signals (e.g., impact) that are distinguishable from formal novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervised learning for novelty classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Train classifiers (SVM, naive Bayes, neural networks, LSTM, BERT) on target patent texts and prior art to predict whether a patent is novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inputs that reflect legally relevant comparisons (e.g., claims and cited prior-art paragraphs). Beware of black-box models lacking explainability. Prefer explainable approaches that output relevant claim–prior-art alignments as rationales (e.g., claim sets with high relevance). Modern LLMs may improve feature extraction and explainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use patent claims as primary content for novelty assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent claims contain essential features of the invention and are the sensible input for automated novelty prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on titles/abstracts for legal novelty prediction; claims better capture features for comparison with prior art. Methods focusing on titles/abstracts are less useful for automated examination processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate patent novelty and technological originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should explicitly distinguish between legal patent novelty (feature-based comparison to prior art) and technological originality (technical advancement or uniqueness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses and evaluation metrics should avoid conflating these concepts; specify which notion is being operationalized and choose data/indicators accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore powerful LLMs for novelty prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate the effectiveness of large language models (e.g., GPT-4) to extract and compare features between target patents and prior art for novelty assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LLMs could address limitations of older embedding methods and improve explicit feature extraction and explainability; prior work largely used older embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability criteria (novelty, non-obviousness/inventiveness, utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability is assessed by whether an invention meets novelty, inventiveness/non-obviousness, and utility requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-obviousness requires a sufficient inventive step beyond what is known and should not be obvious to a person skilled in the art. Utility requires usefulness and practical application. Patentability assessment is more comprehensive and challenging than novelty alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature-decomposition approach for patentability (novelty & non-obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decompose patent claims into features and formulate feature combinations to compare the target patent with prior art for evaluating novelty and non-obviousness following legal definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mathematical-logical approach can align with legal definitions but may face scalability issues (proof-of-concept on single patents) and problems detecting homonyms/synonyms. LLMs can potentially improve effectiveness and efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granting prediction (grant vs terminal rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Predict whether a patent application will be granted or terminally rejected by examiners (a classification task).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for examiners, applicants, and investors. Models should account for complexity and long processing times. Existing baselines (CNNs, BERT) show limited accuracy (<64%); combined text+metadata approaches (e.g., PARCEL) have reached ~75% on some datasets but results are dataset-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine text and metadata for granting prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use both patent texts (abstracts, claims) and metadata (e.g., classifications, dates, assignees) to improve granting prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hybrid frameworks (e.g., contextual bidirectional LSTM for text + network embedding for metadata + attention mechanisms) outperform text-only models. Comparisons across studies require common datasets due to differing data distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation prediction: task definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Predict whether a patent will cause litigation (infringement actions, validity challenges) between parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early identification helps portfolio management. Litigation prediction covers multiple litigation types and often requires integrating various patent and external features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metadata and graph features for litigation prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: In litigation prediction, metadata (number of claims, patent type) and citation graph features have high predictive impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining metadata, claim texts, and graph features can improve performance; metadata often has the highest impact among input types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate lawsuit/company litigation history for prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: Include historical lawsuit records of companies (plaintiffs/defendants) alongside patent content for predicting litigation likelihood between companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models that integrate lawsuit tensors and patent feature vectors can significantly improve precision (reported >10% gain) over text-only approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent patents and companies jointly to capture relations in litigation prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve numerical representations of patents and companies to model complex relations among plaintiffs, defendants, and patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods that capture relational structures show robustness under data sparsity and can increase prediction performance (up to ~10% reported improvements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent valuation: multiple indicators and signal types
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent value depends on scope, dependencies, function, and owner; valuation can be formulated as regression (predict value) or classification (high-quality vs not). Indicators include citations, assigned revenue share, licensing fees, sale values, and other domain-specific signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations correlate with value but have high variability and lag (often arriving years later). Use contemporaneous indicators (revenues, licensing, sales) when available. Consider portfolio context (blocking, freedom-to-operate) and dependency relations between patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent quality dimensions (legal, technological, competitiveness, scientific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate patent quality across multiple dimensions: legal value, technological value, competitiveness value, and scientific value (Hu et al.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extract and transform indicators for each dimension into numerical features for machine learning. Multi-dimensional evaluation captures different facets of patent worth beyond single indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include inventors' reputation as a valuation signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventor reputations (e.g., past productivity, citations, affiliations) can serve as indicators for patent quality and valuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies show inventor reputation can improve quality evaluation; incorporate reputation features where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use text embeddings and citation network models for valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine semantic text features (via CNNs, LSTMs, attention) with graph representations of citation networks (GNNs) to predict patent quality/value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concatenate or fuse textual and network feature vectors to improve predictive performance versus text-only models; attention mechanisms can help emphasize salient parts of texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-task learning for patent valuation and related tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Jointly train models for related tasks (e.g., high-value patent identification and standard-essential patent classification) to exploit shared information and improve performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multi-task learning can provide modest gains (~1–2%) compared to single-task learning when tasks are related.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emerging technology forecasting: indicators and labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Predict whether a patent contains emerging technologies by labeling patent clusters that show evidence of forming a new technological class (e.g., patent class, citation patterns) and using indicators such as class and citation counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approaches include classical classifiers (SVM, Naive Bayes) and generative methods (GANs) to augment data; labeling criteria can be based on external frameworks (e.g., Gartner’s hype cycles). Precision in reported studies ~70–77% with different methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure social impact via external web-article signals for emerging-technology detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Use frequency of patent-related keywords in website articles and other external sources as indicators of social impact and emerging-technology relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multi-source datasets combining patent and web-article data can be used to train models that classify social impact levels; reported accuracies ~74% in one study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology life-cycle prediction via HMM with intrinsic patent indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate technology phases (introduction, growth, maturity, saturation) using models such as hidden Markov models on patent-derived indicators (e.g., patent class, citations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intrinsic patent indicators alone may be insufficient; combine intrinsic data with extrinsic factors (market trends, user acceptance, competitive landscape) for more accurate, holistic forecasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent application trend prediction with dynamic graph representation learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Predict future patent classification codes a company will apply for given its past sequence of patents using dynamic graph representation learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promising but early-stage: improvements over baselines reported, but recall remains low (<20%), indicating substantial room for improvement and company-dependence of patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation recommendation: concept association analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify key concepts in patents and analyze their associations to discover novel combinations and suggest directions for innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods extract technical attributes and find similar-but-distinct attributes to synthesize new ideas; consider intentional variability (e.g., higher sampling temperature) to increase creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology gap detection (TechNet / white-space analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithmically search underdeveloped or unexplored areas in a technology field by building semantic networks of technical terms and identifying white space surrounding focal domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TechNet and semantic-distance measures can guide inference of new technical concepts, but strong dependency on patent terminology and idiosyncratic jargon may limit generality; further research required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-domain analysis for innovation recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Link patents across different technological fields to identify cross-domain techniques and potential breakthrough developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use causal extraction and similarity comparisons across domains to find candidate cross-applications; beware that results can depend heavily on terminology alignment across fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea generation via generative language models
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine-tune generative models (e.g., GPT-2) on patent titles/keywords to produce novel idea titles or suggested innovations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent titles are often generic for legal reasons, limiting the informativeness of generated outputs; careful prompt engineering, domain conditioning, and post-filtering are needed. Consider legal/inventorship implications when AI contributes creative content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/inventorship constraints for AI-generated inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: AI-generated inventions raise legal issues around inventorship and ownership; many jurisdictions (e.g., current US practice) do not consider AI alone as a patentable inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools that generate ideas may need human co-inventors or careful handling of inventorship oaths; evolving legal standards must be monitored when using AI-generated outputs for patenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent summarization: extractive vs abstractive approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarization approaches include extractive methods (selecting sentences verbatim) and abstractive methods (rephrasing and condensing information into fluent summaries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extractive summarization preserves original wording and legal phrasing but may be disjointed and miss implicit information. Abstractive summarization can be more cohesive but risks factual distortion or misrepresenting legal/technical meanings. Transformer-based models and LLMs have improved performance; evaluate carefully for legal fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider target audience when summarizing patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor summaries to audiences (e.g., patent examiners, researchers, development engineers, legal professionals) since information needs and acceptable paraphrasing vary by reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose summarization granularity and style accordingly; technical/legal fidelity is more critical for examiners and attorneys than for general researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent translation: accuracy and legal compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate patent texts between languages to ensure accessibility and compliance with foreign legal requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated translation is well-established in patent offices but must preserve legal meaning and terminology; careful domain adaptation and post-editing are recommended.
